activities.anchor: If an atom were a cathedral
activities.caption: call the emptiness — nucleus versus atom
activities.name: asCathedralEstimate

config.prompt: The nucleus is roughly how many times smaller than the atom that contains it?
config.why: About 100,000 times — an atom is ~0.1 nm across, its nucleus ~10⁻¹⁵ m. A housefly on the cathedral's centre spot, carrying nevertheless more than 99.9 per cent of the mass.
config.context: Your chair is solid because electron clouds refuse to overlap — not because tiny balls touch.

activities.anchor: The modern picture took shape in three famous steps
activities.caption: line up the three famous steps
activities.name: asStepsOrder

config.prompt: The modern atom, step by step — order the milestones:
items: Dalton (1803) — matter consists of indivisible atoms of fixed types
Rutherford (1909–1911) — alpha particles bounce backward: a tiny, dense, positive core
Bohr (1913) — electrons occupy fixed shells at specific energies
config.why: About 1 in 8,000 alpha particles bounced — the shock that forced the nuclear model — and the shell pattern 2, 8, 8 repeats across the first twenty elements.

activities.anchor: is a substance made of one kind of atom only
activities.caption: file each substance — element, compound or mixture
activities.name: asEcmBuckets

config.prompt: Element, compound or mixture? File each:

items.label: water — always 2 H to 1 O, bonded
air — 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, no fixed ratio
iron sulfide — a new black solid the magnet ignores
chlorine — a poisonous green gas of one kind of atom

config.why: Mixtures keep their components' properties and separate physically; compounds need a chemical reaction — fixed ratio, new properties, hard to reverse.

activities.anchor: Three particles do all the work
activities.caption: pair each particle with its charge and mass
activities.name: asParticleMatch

config.prompt: The atom's three particles — pair each with its ledger line:

pairs.right: charge +1, relative mass 1 — the identity card
no charge, mass 1 — the mass trimmer
charge −1, about 1/1836 of a proton — chemistry's decision-maker

config.why: Proton number Z fixes the element; in a neutral atom the electrons exactly equal the protons — the ledger balances.

activities.caption: call the half-life — the archaeologist's clock
activities.name: asCarbonEstimate

config.prompt: Carbon-14 is radioactive. Its half-life is about how many years?
config.why: About 5,700 years — the shrinking fraction of ¹⁴C in dead organic material is what lets archaeologists date ancient wood and bone.
config.context: Hydrogen's trio: ordinary ¹H, deuterium ²H, radioactive tritium ³H.

activities.anchor: the periodic table's atomic masses are not whole numbers
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the weighted average
activities.name: asChlorineCloze

config.text: Chlorine is about 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37, so its relative atomic mass is (75 × 35 + 25 × 37) ÷ 100 = %%0%%. If you ever see a %%1%% atomic mass, an isotope mixture is hiding behind it.
config.hint: Weight the two masses by their percentages; the result is not a whole number.

activities.anchor: it merely persuades whole H₂O molecules to let go of each other
activities.caption: true or false — strong inside, weak outside
activities.name: asBoilJudge

statements.s: Boiling water breaks no O–H bonds — whole H₂O molecules simply let go of each other.
statements.why: Within each molecule the bonds are strong; between molecules there are only weak attractions.
Boiling overcomes only the weak intermolecular attractions — no bonds break.

statements.s: Boiling splits water into hydrogen and oxygen by breaking its covalent bonds.
statements.why: That needs electrolysis or chemistry — a kettle does none of it.

statements.s: Simple molecular substances conduct electricity in any state because their molecules carry charge.
statements.why: Molecules carry no charge — strong inside, weak outside, never conducting is the triple signature.

activities.anchor: A few substances take the covalent bond to the extreme
activities.caption: drag the divider — same element, opposite materials
activities.name: asDiamondCompare

config.prompt: Diamond vs graphite — drag the divider across the carbon:

before.label: diamond
before.text: Every atom bonded to four neighbours in a rigid tetrahedral web — the hardest natural material, melting point above 3,500 °C, an electrical insulator because every electron is locked in a bond.

after.label: graphite
after.text: Each atom bonds to only three, in flat sheets of hexagons with one spare delocalised electron per atom — it conducts (rare for a non-metal), the sheets slide as pencil 'lead' and lubricant.

config.why: Same element, different network, opposite properties: structure is destiny — and silicon dioxide (sand) is a third giant network.
